stat.label: One GPT-4o test: more requirements, lower compliance
stat.detail: This is one test, not a prediction for every model or task. One study also found no general benefit from repository files that repeated discoverable information.

more-is-not-safer.header: A result from one GPT-4o test
more-is-not-safer.description: In one specific GPT-4o test, compliance was 98.7% with one requirement and 85.0% with 19 requirements at once [1]. This result is limited to that test; it does not show that more instructions always reduce compliance. Separately, a study of repository context files did not find a general benefit from restating discoverable information [2].

written-requirements-reduce-variance.title: content-library research, Why do explicit written requirements reduce the variation in LLM output?

gloaguen-evaluating-agents-md.title: Gloaguen, Mündler-Sasahara, Müller, Raychev, Vechev, Evaluating AGENTS.md: Are Repository-Level Context Files Helpful for Coding Agents? (v3, 2026-09-29)

human-manages-the-context.title: Human manages the context
human-manages-the-context.script: You run the bench. You set the context and can limit what the AI may fetch. It can work from there without you overseeing every step, and you can review the result. Think of the AI as a colleague: what would you brief them on, and what would not help?

not-how-the-ai-works-inside.title: Not how the AI works inside
not-how-the-ai-works-inside.script: Your role is to shape the handover and decide what sources are available, not to supervise every action. You can still review what the agent produces. That is why you can learn this without engineering knowledge. So what can happen when the context goes wrong?
